claim: Treatment with phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA) leads to serine phosphorylation of mouse iRhom2 within 15 min.
source: We discovered that treatment with phorbol-12-myristate-13-acetate (PMA), a common activator of TACE-dependent signalling, leads to serine phosphorylation of mouse iRhom2 within 15 min (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a demonstrating phosphoserine detection after PMA treatment.

claim: Mass spectrometric analysis revealed multiple phosphorylated serines within the human iRhom2 cytoplasmic N-terminus without stimulation.
source: Furthermore, even without stimulation, mass spectrometric analysis revealed multiple phosphorylated serines within the human iRhom2 cytoplasmic N-terminus (Figure 1b; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 a-b.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1b and supplementary figures.

claim: The iRhom2 N-terminus is subject to a basal level of phosphorylation, which is enhanced by a stimulator of TACE enzyme activity.
source: Combined, this indicates that the iRhom2 N-terminus is subject to a basal level of phosphorylation, which is enhanced by a stimulator of TACE enzyme activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of basal phosphorylation detected by mass spectrometry and enhanced phosphorylation upon PMA stimulation.

claim: iRhom2pDEAD rescued TACE maturation to the same extent as iRhom2WT in iRhom1/2 double knock-out MEFs.
source: Expression of iRhom2pDEAD in iRhom1/2 double knock-out (DKO) MEFs rescued TACE maturation to the same extent as iRhom2WT (Figure 1d, grey arrowhead).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 1d showing mature TACE levels.

claim: iRhom2 phosphorylation is not essential for the maturation of TACE.
source: Therefore iRhom2 phosphorylation is not essential for the maturation of TACE, suggesting that any phosphorylation-dependent function is restricted to an unknown post-TACE maturation role of iRhom2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that iRhom2pDEAD supports TACE maturation as well as wild-type.

claim: A form of iRhom2 C-terminally tagged with a KDEL motif did not support TACE maturation.
source: Notably, a form of iRhom2 C-terminally tagged with a KDEL motif (Munro and Pelham, 1987), which enhances ER retrieval from the cis-Golgi, did not support TACE maturation (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 a-c
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1d and supplementary figures, with citation to prior work on KDEL function.

claim: iRhom2 itself must be trafficked beyond the ER to promote TACE maturation.
source: Notably, a form of iRhom2 C-terminally tagged with a KDEL motif (Munro and Pelham, 1987), which enhances ER retrieval from the cis-Golgi, did not support TACE maturation (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2 a-c, implying that iRhom2 itself must be trafficked beyond the ER to promote TACE maturation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ER-retained iRhom2KDEL cannot support TACE maturation.

claim: iRhom2WT and iRhom2pDEAD were both detected in the Golgi apparatus, co-localising with the cis-Golgi marker GM130.
source: In support of the conclusion that iRhom2 phosphorylation does not control ER-to-Golgi trafficking of TACE, iRhom2WT and iRhom2pDEAD, but not iRhom2KDEL, were both detected in the Golgi apparatus, co-localising with the cis-Golgi marker GM130 (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1e showing colocalization.

claim: iRhom2 can reach the cell surface.
source: Finally, consistent with a previous report (Maney et al., 2015), we found that iRhom2 can reach the cell surface: using cell surface biotinylation we detected both iRhom2WT and iRhom2pDEAD at the plasma membrane (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by cell surface biotinylation data in Figure 1f and citation to prior work.

claim: The ER-to-Golgi traffic of iRhom2 and TACE is independent of iRhom2 N-terminal phosphorylation.
source: Overall, this demonstrates that iRhom2 is not limited to the early secretory pathway, but also reaches the plasma membrane, and that the ER-to-Golgi traffic of iRhom2 and TACE is independent of iRhom2 N-terminal phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple observations showing that phosphorylation-deficient mutants traffic normally.

claim: iRhom2pDEAD was greatly impaired in its ability to promote TACE-dependent shedding of EGF-like ligands in response to PMA activation.
source: We found that iRhom2pDEAD was greatly impaired in its ability to promote TACE-dependent shedding of EGF-like ligands (Figure 1g–h) and TNFα (Figure 1i) in response to PMA activation.
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase shedding assay data in Figures 1g-h.

claim: iRhom2pDEAD was greatly impaired in its ability to promote TACE-dependent shedding of TNFα in response to PMA activation.
source: We found that iRhom2pDEAD was greatly impaired in its ability to promote TACE-dependent shedding of EGF-like ligands (Figure 1g–h) and TNFα (Figure 1i) in response to PMA activation.
evidence: Supported by alkaline phosphatase shedding assay data in Figure 1i.

claim: The requirement for iRhom2 phosphorylation was specific to TACE substrates since the shedding of EGF or betacellulin, which depends on ADAM10, was unaffected by absence of iRhom2 phosphorylation.
source: The requirement for iRhom2 phosphorylation was specific to TACE substrates since the shedding of EGF or betacellulin, which depends on the related protease ADAM10 (Sahin et al., 2004), was unaffected by absence of iRhom2 phosphorylation (Figure 1j).
evidence: Supported by shedding assay data in Figure 1j and citation to prior work on ADAM10 substrate specificity.

claim: Phosphorylation of the iRhom2 N-terminus specifically controls the proteolytic activity of mature TACE at the cell surface.
source: We conclude that phosphorylation of the iRhom2 N-terminus does not regulate its role of controlling ER-to-Golgi trafficking and maturation of TACE, but instead specifically controls the proteolytic activity of mature TACE at the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of observations showing normal TACE maturation but impaired activity with phosphorylation-deficient mutants.

claim: Three distinct sites in iRhom2 strongly contribute to PMA-induced TACE-dependent shedding: Site1 comprises S58 and S60; Site2 comprises S83, S85, and S87; and Site3 comprises S357, S359, S360 and T361.
source: This revealed three distinct sites that strongly contribute to PMA-induced TACE-dependent shedding: Site1 comprises S58 and S60; Site2 comprises S83, S85, and S87; and Site3 comprises S357, S359, S360 and T361 (Figure 2a - highlighted in red text, and Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by alanine-scanning mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2a and related figures.

claim: The three phosphorylation sites additively regulate TACE-dependent shedding of both TGFα and TNFα.
source: Assessment of the three phosphorylation site mutants individually (iRhom2Site1, iRhom2Site2 and iRhom2Site3) and in combination (iRhom2Site1-3) reveals that they additively regulate TACE-dependent shedding of both TGFα and TNFα (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by shedding assay data in Figures 2b and 2c.

claim: GPCR stimulation with histamine triggers TACE-dependent release of amphiregulin and TGFα in an iRhom2 phosphorylation-dependent manner.
source: PMA is not a physiological trigger for TACE activity, so to confirm the physiological significance of our observations, we showed that GPCR stimulation with histamine triggers TACE-dependent release of amphiregulin and TGFα in an iRhom2 phosphorylation-dependent manner (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by shedding assay data with histamine stimulation in Figure 2d.

claim: Stimulated phosphorylation of iRhom2 is lost upon simultaneous alanine mutation of all three of the identified sites required for TACE activity.
source: Finally, we confirmed that stimulated phosphorylation of iRhom2 is lost upon simultaneous alanine mutation of all three of the identified sites required for TACE activity (Figure 2e).
evidence: Supported by phosphoserine immunoblot data in Figure 2e.

claim: Multiple 14-3-3 family proteins bind to the cytoplasmic domain of iRhom2.
source: In a proteomic screen for proteins that interact with iRhom2, we identified multiple 14-3-3 family proteins binding to the cytoplasmic domain (Figure 2f).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 2f.

claim: 14-3-3 proteins strongly bind to the N-terminus of iRhom2 upon PMA stimulation, in a phosphorylation-dependent manner.
source: Using both iRhom2pDEAD and iRhom2Site1-3, we found that 14-3-3 proteins strongly bind to the N-terminus of iRhom2 upon PMA stimulation, in a phosphorylation-dependent manner (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 2g.

claim: All 14-3-3 isoforms bound phosphorylated iRhom2 apart from 14-3-3α/β, although binding to 14-3-3ζ was weak.
source: Of the seven 14-3-3 isoforms, we could confirm by western blot that all bound phosphorylated iRhom2 apart from 14-3-3α/β, although binding to 14-3-3ζ was weak (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–f; 14-3-3σ antibody failed, data not shown).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in supplementary figures.

claim: iRhom2KDEL recruited 14-3-3 proteins upon stimulation with PMA.
source: Last, we found that the ER-Golgi retention mutant, iRhom2KDEL, also recruited 14-3-3 proteins upon stimulation with PMA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g), indicating that iRhom2 is phosphorylated throughout the secretory pathway.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in supplementary figure 1g.

claim: iRhom2 is phosphorylated throughout the secretory pathway.
source: Last, we found that the ER-Golgi retention mutant, iRhom2KDEL, also recruited 14-3-3 proteins upon stimulation with PMA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g), indicating that iRhom2 is phosphorylated throughout the secretory pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ER-retained iRhom2KDEL can still be phosphorylated and recruit 14-3-3.

claim: Mass spectrometry screen reproducibly identified ribosomal protein S6 kinase alpha-3 (RSK3) and extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1/2 (ERK1/2) as potential binding partners of iRhom2.
source: Our mass spectrometry screen reproducibly identified ribosomal protein S6 kinase alpha-3 (RSK3) and extracellular signal-regulated kinases 1/2 (ERK1/2, also known as MAPK3/1 respectively) as potential binding partners of iRhom2 (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 3a.

claim: PMA stimulated amphiregulin release is insensitive to RSK inhibition, but reduced upon MEK1/2 inhibition.
source: This experiment demonstrated that PMA stimulated amphiregulin release is insensitive to RSK inhibition, but reduced upon MEK1/2 inhibition (Figure 3b), in line with a previous study (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by shedding assay data with kinase inhibitors in Figure 3b and citation to prior work.

claim: Histamine-stimulated release of amphiregulin by TACE was inhibited by U0126.
source: We also tested more physiological stimulation by the GPCR agonist histamine. In this case, too, stimulated release of amphiregulin by TACE was inhibited by U0126 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by shedding assay data with histamine and U0126 in Figure 3c.

claim: Both PMA and histamine treatments cause upregulated ERK1/2 activity, monitored through enhanced ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
source: Importantly, we showed that both PMA and histamine treatments indeed do cause upregulated ERK1/2 activity, monitored through enhanced ERK1/2 phosphorylation (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing phospho-ERK1/2 in Figures 3d-f.

claim: Stimulated ERK1/2 phosphorylation is unaffected in DKO MEFs expressing the iRhom2Site1-3 transgene.
source: These results are consistent with iRhom2 phosphorylation being downstream of ERK1/2, and this was confirmed by the observation that stimulated ERK1/2 phosphorylation is unaffected in DKO MEFs expressing the iRhom2Site1-3 transgene (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figures 3e-f showing ERK phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of iRhom2 is dependent on MEK1/2 activity.
source: First, we show that phosphorylation of iRhom2 is dependent on MEK1/2 activity (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by phosphoserine immunoblot data with U0126 treatment in Figure 3d.

claim: PMA and histamine induced recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins to iRhom2 is abrogated by MEK1/2 inhibition with U0126.
source: Second, PMA and histamine induced recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins to iRhom2 is abrogated by MEK1/2 inhibition with U0126 (Figure 3d–f).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with U0126 treatment in Figures 3d-f.

claim: iRhom2 is phosphorylated downstream of activated ERK signalling.
source: We conclude from these data that iRhom2 is phosphorylated downstream of activated ERK signalling, and that the activity of these kinases is required for 14-3-3 recruitment to the N-terminus of iRhom2 and TACE-dependent shedding.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of observations showing ERK-dependent iRhom2 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 recruitment.

claim: The activity of ERK kinases is required for 14-3-3 recruitment to the N-terminus of iRhom2 and TACE-dependent shedding.
source: We conclude from these data that iRhom2 is phosphorylated downstream of activated ERK signalling, and that the activity of these kinases is required for 14-3-3 recruitment to the N-terminus of iRhom2 and TACE-dependent shedding.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of observations showing that MEK/ERK inhibition blocks both 14-3-3 recruitment and TACE shedding.

claim: iRhom2 lacking its cytoplasmic domain (iRhom2∆NT) did not bind mature TACE.
source: Strikingly, iRhom2 lacking its cytoplasmic domain (iRhom2∆NT) did not bind mature TACE, although its binding to immature TACE was unaffected (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4a.

claim: iRhom2∆NT binding to immature TACE was unaffected.
source: Strikingly, iRhom2 lacking its cytoplasmic domain (iRhom2∆NT) did not bind mature TACE, although its binding to immature TACE was unaffected (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4a.

claim: Deletion of the iRhom homology domain (iRhom2∆IRHD) strongly impaired immature TACE binding in DKO MEFs.
source: In contrast, deletion of the iRhom homology domain (iRhom2∆IRHD, Figure 1c) strongly impaired immature TACE binding in DKO MEFs (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4b.

claim: The N-terminus of iRhom2 is specifically required for its interaction with mature TACE.
source: These data reveal that the N-terminus of iRhom2 is specifically required for its interaction with mature TACE, but is not required for iRhom2 binding to the immature form of TACE, which instead depends on the iRhom2 IRHD.
evidence: Inferred from the differential binding patterns of iRhom2∆NT and iRhom2∆IRHD to mature and immature TACE.

claim: iRhom2 binding to the immature form of TACE depends on the iRhom2 IRHD.
source: These data reveal that the N-terminus of iRhom2 is specifically required for its interaction with mature TACE, but is not required for iRhom2 binding to the immature form of TACE, which instead depends on the iRhom2 IRHD.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that iRhom2∆IRHD cannot bind immature TACE.

claim: iRhom2∆NT was unable to support TACE maturation.
source: Despite its ability to bind immature TACE, iRhom2∆NT was unable to support TACE maturation (Figure 4c, compare lanes 4 and 7).
evidence: Supported by ConA enrichment data in Figure 4c.

claim: iRhom2∆NT can support TACE maturation, but in the absence of the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain, mature TACE is unstable and degraded in lysosomes.
source: This showed that iRhom2∆NT can in fact support TACE maturation, but in the absence of the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain, mature TACE is unstable and degraded in lysosomes (Figure 4c, compare lanes 7 and 8; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by data showing rescue of mature TACE with bafilomycin A1 treatment in Figure 4c.

claim: The iRhom2 N-terminus regulates the post-Golgi stability of mature TACE.
source: This result uncovers an unanticipated molecular function for iRhom2, regulating the post-Golgi stability of mature TACE.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mature TACE is degraded in lysosomes without the iRhom2 N-terminus.

claim: iRhom2∆IRHD did not support TACE maturation, and the absence of mature TACE was not rescued by degradation inhibitors.
source: By comparison, iRhom2∆IRHD, which is strongly impaired in its ability to bind immature TACE, did not support TACE maturation: the absence of mature TACE was not rescued by either of the degradation inhibitors (Figure 4c, compare lanes 4 and 10–12).
evidence: Supported by ConA enrichment data with degradation inhibitors in Figure 4c.

claim: The iRhom2 IRHD is essential for the ER-to-Golgi traffic and maturation of TACE.
source: This implies that, unlike the N-terminus, the iRhom2 IRHD is essential for the ER-to-Golgi traffic and maturation of TACE, further distinguishing the newly discovered post-Golgi function of iRhom2 from its previously reported ER-to-Golgi trafficking role.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that iRhom2∆IRHD cannot support TACE maturation even with degradation inhibitors.

claim: The iRhom2 cytoplasmic N-terminus is not needed for ER-to-Golgi trafficking and maturation of TACE, but instead mediates its binding to mature TACE at the plasma membrane.
source: Collectively, these results show that the iRhom2 cytoplasmic N-terminus is not needed for ER-to-Golgi trafficking and maturation of TACE, but instead mediates its binding to mature TACE at the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of observations about iRhom2∆NT function.

claim: iRhom2 N-terminus binding stabilises TACE by preventing its lysosomal degradation.
source: This binding stabilises TACE by preventing its lysosomal degradation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mature TACE is degraded in lysosomes without the iRhom2 N-terminus.

claim: iRhom2R18 showed constitutive recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins.
source: iRhom2R18 not only showed constitutive recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins (Figure 5b) but also constitutively elevated TACE activity (Figure 5c), indicating that 14-3-3 recruitment to the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain is indeed sufficient to activate the shedding activity of TACE.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5b.

claim: iRhom2R18 showed constitutively elevated TACE activity.
source: iRhom2R18 not only showed constitutive recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins (Figure 5b) but also constitutively elevated TACE activity (Figure 5c), indicating that 14-3-3 recruitment to the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain is indeed sufficient to activate the shedding activity of TACE.
evidence: Supported by shedding assay data in Figure 5c.

claim: 14-3-3 recruitment to the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain is sufficient to activate the shedding activity of TACE.
source: iRhom2R18 not only showed constitutive recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins (Figure 5b) but also constitutively elevated TACE activity (Figure 5c), indicating that 14-3-3 recruitment to the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain is indeed sufficient to activate the shedding activity of TACE.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constitutive 14-3-3 binding leads to constitutive TACE activity.

claim: iRhom2R18 supported TACE maturation to the same extent as iRhom2WT.
source: Elevated levels of mature TACE did not cause this increase in shedding, as iRhom2R18 supported TACE maturation to the same extent as iRhom2WT (Figure 5d).
evidence: Supported by ConA enrichment data in Figure 5d.

claim: The constitutive 14-3-3 binding form binds mature TACE less well than iRhom2WT.
source: Significantly, we found that this constitutive 14-3-3 binding form binds mature TACE less well than iRhom2WT (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5e.

claim: Reduction of binding was not caused simply by the loss of the Site 1 and 2 phosphorylation sites in iRhom2R18, as iRhom2Site1-2 could still bind to mature TACE normally.
source: Reduction of binding was not caused simply by the loss of the Site 1 and 2 phosphorylation sites in iRhom2R18, as iRhom2Site1-2 could still bind to mature TACE normally (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5e.

claim: 14-3-3 recruitment to iRhom2 modifies the complex to weaken mature TACE binding.
source: This suggests that 14-3-3 recruitment to iRhom2 modifies the complex to weaken mature TACE binding.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that constitutive 14-3-3 binding reduces TACE binding.

claim: iRhom2 and mature TACE form a complex at the plasma membrane.
source: This showed that iRhom2 and mature TACE do indeed form a complex at the plasma membrane, and that this interaction is reduced upon PMA stimulation (Figure 5f, compare the reduction in TACE co-immunoprecipitation in lanes 3 and 4, and in lanes 5 and 6; relative to total surface levels of mature TACE in lanes 9–12).
evidence: Supported by plasma membrane immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5f.

claim: The interaction between iRhom2 and mature TACE at the plasma membrane is reduced upon PMA stimulation.
source: This showed that iRhom2 and mature TACE do indeed form a complex at the plasma membrane, and that this interaction is reduced upon PMA stimulation (Figure 5f, compare the reduction in TACE co-immunoprecipitation in lanes 3 and 4, and in lanes 5 and 6; relative to total surface levels of mature TACE in lanes 9–12).
evidence: Supported by plasma membrane immunoprecipitation data in Figure 5f.

claim: The complex between iRhom2 and TACE is more stable with the non-phosphorylatable mutant, iRhom2Site1-3.
source: Furthermore, the complex is more stable with the non-phosphorylatable mutant, iRhom2Site1-3 (Figure 5f, see graph for quantification).
evidence: Supported by plasma membrane immunoprecipitation data and quantification in Figure 5f.

claim: A more stable iRhom2-TACE complex leads to less TACE activity.
source: These data also make the converse point: a more stable iRhom2-TACE complex leads to less TACE activity.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between stable complex formation and reduced TACE activity.

claim: iRhom2 binds to and stabilises mature TACE at the plasma membrane but this complex inhibits TACE activity.
source: Overall, these results lead us to propose a new signalling mechanism that governs TACE activity. iRhom2 binds to and stabilises mature TACE at the plasma membrane but this complex inhibits TACE activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of observations about iRhom2-TACE complex formation and activity.

claim: Phosphorylation of the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain drives the recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins, weakening the interaction between iRhom2 and TACE, an essential requirement for TACE proteolytic activity as a shedding enzyme.
source: Phosphorylation of the iRhom2 cytoplasmic domain drives the recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins, weakening the interaction between iRhom2 and TACE, an essential requirement for TACE proteolytic activity as a shedding enzyme.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of observations about phosphorylation, 14-3-3 binding, complex weakening, and TACE activity.

claim: iRhom2 is the sole iRhom in macrophages.
source: iRhom2 is the sole iRhom in macrophages, and iRhom2 KO mice are viable but compromised in macrophage secretion of TNFα, with consequent inflammatory defects (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012; Siggs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on iRhom2 expression and function in macrophages.

claim: iRhom2 KO mice are viable but compromised in macrophage secretion of TNFα, with consequent inflammatory defects.
source: iRhom2 is the sole iRhom in macrophages, and iRhom2 KO mice are viable but compromised in macrophage secretion of TNFα, with consequent inflammatory defects (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012; Siggs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on iRhom2 knockout mice.

claim: TACE maturation was rescued by both iRhom2WT and iRhom2Site1-3 in primary bone marrow-derived macrophages from iRhom2 KO mice.
source: TACE maturation was rescued by both constructs, indicating that, as in MEFs, phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic domain of iRhom2 is not needed for TACE trafficking and maturation in vivo (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by ConA enrichment data from primary macrophages in Figure 6a.

claim: Phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic domain of iRhom2 is not needed for TACE trafficking and maturation in vivo.
source: TACE maturation was rescued by both constructs, indicating that, as in MEFs, phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic domain of iRhom2 is not needed for TACE trafficking and maturation in vivo (Figure 6a).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that phosphorylation-deficient mutant rescues TACE maturation in primary macrophages.

claim: In response to PMA activation or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) treatment, both iRhom2 serine phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding occur in primary macrophages.
source: Furthermore, in response to PMA activation or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) treatment (which mimics bacterial infection), we observed both iRhom2 serine phosphorylation, and 14-3-3 binding in primary macrophages (Figure 6b and Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation data from primary macrophages in Figures 6b and 6c.

claim: LPS-triggered shedding of TNFα from iRhom2 KO macrophages was rescued by iRhom2WT, but not by its phospho-deficient form, iRhom2Site1-3.
source: Finally, we found that LPS-triggered shedding of TNFα from iRhom2 KO macrophages was rescued by iRhom2WT, but not by its phospho-deficient form, iRhom2Site1-3 (Figure 6d).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data from primary macrophages in Figure 6d.

claim: iRhom2 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding mediate regulation of TACE activity in vivo.
source: We conclude that iRhom2 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding mediate regulation of TACE activity in vivo, and therefore represent a pathophysiologically relevant mechanism that controls macrophage-mediated inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the observations in primary macrophages showing phosphorylation-dependent TNFα release.

claim: iRhom2 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding represent a pathophysiologically relevant mechanism that controls macrophage-mediated inflammation.
source: We conclude that iRhom2 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding mediate regulation of TACE activity in vivo, and therefore represent a pathophysiologically relevant mechanism that controls macrophage-mediated inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the observations in primary macrophages showing phosphorylation-dependent TNFα release.

claim: iRhom2 controls transport of TACE from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where removal of its pro-domain by pro-protein convertases such as furin occurs.
source: We reported that iRhoms control transport of TACE from the ER to the Golgi apparatus, where removal of its pro-domain by pro-protein convertases such as furin occurs (Endres et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on furin cleavage.

claim: iRhoms regulate the conversion of TACE from an inactive immature form to a mature proteolytically competent shedding enzyme.
source: In this way, iRhoms regulate the conversion of TACE from an inactive immature form to a mature proteolytically competent shedding enzyme (Adrain and Freeman, 2012; Freeman, 2014; Lemberg and Adrain, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on iRhom function.

claim: Without iRhoms there is no TACE maturation and therefore no TACE activity.
source: Without iRhoms there is no TACE maturation and therefore no TACE activity (Christova et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on iRhom requirement for TACE.

claim: Macrophages express only iRhom2.
source: Of the two mammalian iRhoms, iRhom1 is broadly expressed, whereas macrophages express only iRhom2.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about iRhom expression patterns.

claim: Macrophages are the major TNFα-releasing cell type.
source: Since macrophages are the major TNFα-releasing cell type (Parameswaran and Patial, 2010), this makes iRhom2 an important regulator of inflammation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on macrophage TNFα production.

claim: iRhom2 knock-out mice have profound inflammatory defects, are sensitive to bacterial infection and are resistant to LPS-induced toxic shock and the development of inflammatory arthritis.
source: Accordingly iRhom2 knock-out mice have profound inflammatory defects, are sensitive to bacterial infection and are resistant to LPS-induced toxic shock and the development of inflammatory arthritis (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012; Issuree et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on iRhom2 knockout mice phenotypes.

claim: iRhom2 was shown to modulate innate immunity to DNA viruses by regulating the ER-to-Golgi transport and the stability of the immune adaptor STING.
source: More recently iRhom2 was shown to modulate innate immunity to DNA viruses by regulating the ER-to-Golgi transport and the stability of the immune adaptor STING (Luo et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on iRhom2 and STING.

claim: TACE is first synthesised in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) as an immature form containing an inhibitory pro-domain that prevents its proteolytic activity.
source: TACE is first synthesised in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) as an immature form containing an inhibitory pro-domain that prevents its proteolytic activity.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about TACE biosynthesis.

claim: TACE is a primary shedding enzyme that regulates multiple signalling pathways through its ability to cleave and release numerous membrane-tethered signalling ligands and receptors.
source: TACE (also known as ADAM17) is a primary shedding enzyme and as such regulates multiple signalling pathways through its ability to cleave and release numerous membrane-tethered signalling ligands and receptors (Peschon et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work on TACE function.

claim: TACE controls the shedding of TNFα, the principal inflammatory cytokine.
source: Of particular interest, it controls the shedding of TNFα, the principal inflammatory cytokine (Black et al., 1997; Moss et al., 1997), amphiregulin, TGFα and most other ligands of the epidermal growth factor (EGF) family (Sunnarborg et al., 2002; Sahin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on TACE substrates.

claim: TACE controls the shedding of amphiregulin, TGFα and most other ligands of the epidermal growth factor (EGF) family.
source: Of particular interest, it controls the shedding of TNFα, the principal inflammatory cytokine (Black et al., 1997; Moss et al., 1997), amphiregulin, TGFα and most other ligands of the epidermal growth factor (EGF) family (Sunnarborg et al., 2002; Sahin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on TACE substrates.

claim: iRhoms act downstream of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signalling in the transactivation of EGFR signalling.
source: Moreover, iRhoms act downstream of G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) signalling in the transactivation of EGFR signalling (Christova et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on iRhom function in GPCR signaling.

claim: TACE-induced ligand shedding is rapid: it is activated within ten minutes by physiological and pharmacological stimulation.
source: Importantly, TACE-induced ligand shedding is rapid: it is activated within ten minutes by physiological and pharmacological stimulation (Le Gall et al., 2010), and this is compatible with the timescale on which iRhoms have been reported to influence TACE substrate selection (Maretzky et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on TACE activation kinetics.

claim: The speed of TACE activation is not easily reconciled with its relatively slow ER-to-Golgi trafficking and maturation (3–6 hr).
